Laboratory studies of the Brown rat (Rattus norvegicus) provide detailed insights into its reproductive biology, with many measurements taken under controlled thermal conditions. When maintained at a standard body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], gestation in this species lasts approximately 20 days [tg = approximately 20 days], a relatively brief period that facilitates rapid population turnover. The altricial neonates emerge weighing roughly 7 grams [Wwb = roughly 7 grams], a modest birth mass that reflects the energetic constraints of producing a large litter during a short pregnancy. This initial size belies the substantial growth trajectory the pups will undergo during the early postnatal period. Females typically achieve a moderate litter size of 9 to 10 pups per litter [N_R_i = 9 to 10 pups per litter], and under optimal laboratory conditions they can produce roughly 3.7 litters annually [F_R_i = roughly 3.7 litters annually], generating a considerable annual reproductive output. These reproductive parameters, recorded at the species' core temperature, underscore the prodigious fecundity that characterizes this widespread murid rodent.

The developmental milestones of young rats also unfold at a rapid pace when animals are reared under standard conditions at 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. Weaning, marking the transition from exclusive milk dependence to solid food consumption, occurs at approximately 17.5 days after birth [tx = approximately 17.5 days after birth], a point at which the pups have achieved sufficient somatic development to process at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C] an adult diet. Shortly thereafter, the pre-weaning juvenile period concludes, and the young enter a phase of independent foraging. The onset of reproductive capability follows several weeks later; in female Sprague-Dawley individuals, a commonly studied laboratory strain, puberty is attained at 42 days after birth [tp = 42 days after birth] under the same thermal regime at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This relatively early maturation, coupled with the short gestation interval, contributes to the species' capacity for explosive population growth when resources are abundant. The synchronized timing of weaning and pubertal development highlights the tight coordination between somatic growth and reproductive physiology in this species.

In adulthood, the Brown rat reaches a considerable size, with total body length from nose to tail tip extending to 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters] in large individuals. The ultimate wet weight corresponding to this skeletal dimension is approximately 820 grams [Wwi = approximately 820 grams], placing the species among the larger members of the genus Rattus. Before attaining this asymptotic mass, females typically achieve a wet weight at puberty of around 151.8 grams [Wwp = around 151.8 grams] at the time of conception, as documented in Sprague-Dawley stock records. This pubertal weight represents only about 18.5% of the final adult mass, indicating that considerable somatic growth continues long after reproductive maturity has been reached. Such a pattern is common in mammalian species where selection favors early reproduction, even at the cost of competing with ongoing growth. The substantial divergence between pubertal and ultimate body mass underscores the prolonged period of tissue accretion that characterizes this species' life history.

Longevity in the Brown rat is notably extended under the protective conditions of a thermoneutral laboratory environment at 37 °C [T = 37 °C], with the maximum lifespan recorded at approximately 18 years [am = approximately 18 years] in some captive populations. This lifespan is remarkably long for a rodent of this body size, exceeding predictions based on general mammalian allometric relationships and reflecting the species' adaptation to a relatively low-mortality ecological niche in human-associated habitats. In natural settings, however, mortality from predation, disease, and food scarcity typically truncates survival considerably, and few individuals approach this physiological ceiling. The species' ability to maintain reproductive function across most of the adult lifespan, in combination with its high fecundity and rapid maturation, allows populations to recover quickly from density reductions. This longevity, when expressed in relation to the abbreviated generation time, produces a life history strategy that balances high replacement rates with the capacity for extended reproductive output over many consecutive breeding cycles.

Examining the Brown rat's overall life history reveals a syndrome built around rapid maturation, high fecundity, and considerable maximum lifespan. The reproductive rate, a key determinant of population dynamics, is best understood from its components: females produce 9 to 10 pups per litter [N_R_i = 9 to 10 pups per litter] and approximately 3.7 litters annually [F_R_i = approximately 3.7 litters annually] under optimal conditions at a sustained core temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This prodigious output, when contrasted with the relatively long potential lifespan of 18 years [am = 18 years], illustrates the species' remarkable capacity for population expansion at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. Comparative studies with other murid rodents show that Rattus norvegicus occupies an extreme position along the fast-slow continuum, combining one of the shortest gestation periods for its size with one of the longest recorded lifespans among its peers.
